806.title: Ali's words
806.hook: sermons and sayings attributed to Ali, gathered in Nahj al-Balagha, are especially treasured by Shia Muslims
806.howItsDone: Shia Muslims read Nahj al-Balagha for guidance, study it in seminaries and quote it in sermons; Sunni readers also study it, especially for its Arabic style.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ali ibn Abi Talib: Haydar the lion, and Abu Turab asleep in the dust. Your line was the lion and the scholar. What did you take one layer deeper? Day eight hundred six.

A governor is about to leave for his new province, and a letter is put in his hands. It tells him how to treat the people he'll rule. And somewhere in it is a line worth stopping on: people are of two kinds. Either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation. The letter is attributed to Ali, written to Malik al-Ashtar as he went to govern Egypt. It's one of many pieces gathered in a single book. Today: Ali's words.
screen: `A LETTER TO A GOVERNOR.` → `TWO KINDS OF PEOPLE.` → `A BROTHER, OR AN EQUAL.`

segments.voice: The book is called Nahj al-Balagha, the path of eloquence. Its compiler gathered sermons, letters and short sayings attributed to Ali, arranged in those three parts. Shia Muslims treasure it especially, reading it alongside the Qur'an and the hadith as words from their first Imam. Sunni readers have also prized it, often for the beauty of its Arabic, and some scholars question whether every piece in it goes back to Ali himself. So this path says attributed, and means it. Now, the words. Take the line to the governor again. Either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation. It leaves nobody out. If someone shares your religion, they're your brother or sister. If they don't, they still came from the same Maker as you, and they're owed the same justice. For a ruler about to hold power over many kinds of people, that's a job description. A short saying is about worth: the value of each person lies in what they do well. The saying doesn't name family or wealth. Only what they do well. And a long letter of advice to his son al-Hasan includes this, in paraphrase: make yourself the measure between you and others. Want for them what you want for yourself, and dislike for them what you dislike for yourself. Don't be anyone's slave when God made you free. Listen to the sound of all three. They're short enough to carry. This is where the first circle closes: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, four men around the Prophet, each remembered in his own way.
screen: `NAHJ AL-BALAGHA: THE PATH OF ELOQUENCE.` · `A BROTHER IN FAITH, OR AN EQUAL IN CREATION.` · `WORTH IS WHAT YOU DO WELL.` · `MAKE YOURSELF THE MEASURE.` · then, large: `WORDS FROM ALI.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one saying attributed to Ali. Sit, and breathe. Choose one of the three you just heard. A brother in faith, or an equal in creation. Worth is what you do well. Make yourself the measure. Say it slowly in your head. Then bring to mind one person you'll meet today, and hold the saying up to them. What would it change about how you treat them? Stay with that one line and that one person. The bell holds the time.
Ali's words. Sermons, letters and sayings attributed to Ali, known as Abu Turab,, gathered in Nahj al-Balagha and especially treasured by Shia Muslims. Today's word.
Your line: words from Ali. Today, when someone is hard to like, try the letter: a brother in faith, or an equal in creation. Day eight hundred six.

807.title: Khadijah, first believer
807.hook: the angel brings a message for one woman alone: greetings of peace from her Lord (Bukhari)
807.howItsDone: Muslims honor Khadijah among the mothers of the believers, and her words on the night of the first revelation, from Sahih al-Bukhari, are often retold when the beginning of the revelation is taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ali's words: a brother in faith, or an equal in creation. Your line was words from Ali. Who did you try the letter on? Today a new stretch begins: the mothers of the believers. Day eight hundred seven.

Peace, from her Lord. In a report preserved by Bukhari, the angel Jibril says to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: here is Khadijah, coming to you with a vessel of food. When she reaches you, give her greetings of peace from her Lord, and from me. A message from heaven, addressed to one person by name, about to arrive with her hands full. The Qur'an calls the Prophet's wives mothers of the believers. Today the first of them: Khadijah.
screen: `SHE COMES WITH A VESSEL OF FOOD.` → `JIBRIL NAMES HER.` → `PEACE FROM HER LORD.`

segments.voice: First, the title of this stretch. Surah thirty-three, verse six, in Pickthall: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their selves, and his wives are (as) their mothers." So for the next days we meet them one at a time. Why is Khadijah greeted like this? Go back to the night everything began. Bukhari's account of the first revelation has the Prophet coming home from the cave of Hira shaking, saying: cover me, cover me. He tells Khadijah he fears for himself. And she answers him, not with a theory, but with a list of what she has watched him do. Never, she says. By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep the ties of family. You carry the burden of the weak. You give to those who have nothing. You honor your guest. You stand by people when trouble comes. Then she takes him to her cousin Waraqah, who knew the earlier scriptures, to hear what it might mean. Tradition remembers her as the first to believe him. Notice how she believed: by trusting the character she knew, when he himself was afraid. And notice how she was remembered. Aisha says in Bukhari that she never felt jealous of any woman the way she did of Khadijah, though she never saw her, because the Prophet spoke of her so often, and would send gifts to her friends. Then the greeting itself. In the same report, Jibril adds glad news: a house in Paradise for her, made of hollow pearl, with no noise in it and no weariness. The one who steadied him in a frightening night is promised a place of quiet. Greeted by her Lord.

Do what Khadijah did: make a short list. One thing you have seen them do. A second. A third. Hold each one for a breath. If you pray, you can ask peace for them by name. If not, simply let the list stand, and notice who is on it. The bell holds the time.

808.title: Sawdah, who made him smile
808.hook: a widow who joins his household after Khadijah, remembered for her humor and her open hand
808.carry: the one who made him smile
808.howItsDone: Muslims count Sawdah bint Zam'ah among the mothers of the believers; the reports of her giving her day to Aisha and her early leaving at Muzdalifah come from Sahih al-Bukhari, and the stories of her humor from the early biographers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khadijah, the one who steadied him, and the peace sent to her. Your line was: greeted by her lord. Did you tell a faithful person what you've seen them do? Day eight hundred eight.

A long night prayer. Bowing, and bowing, and still bowing. Afterward, a woman of his household who prayed behind him comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and says: I prayed behind you last night, and you bowed so long I held my nose, in case it started to bleed. And he laughs. That small joke is how Ibn Sa'd's book of early lives remembers her. She was a widow, the biographers say, who came into his household after Khadijah died, in a house that had just lost its center. Today: Sawdah.
screen: `A VERY LONG BOW.` → `I HELD MY NOSE.` → `AND HE LAUGHED.`

segments.voice: Sawdah doesn't arrive in the story with a battle or a revelation attached to her name. She arrives in the ordinary rooms of a grieving home, and she brings lightness into them. The reports about her are small, and that is the point of them. First, her humor. The joke about the long bow is a report in Ibn Sa'd, not in the two Sahih collections, so hold it as a story the early biographers kept. It shows something worth keeping: a person who could make the Prophet laugh about a long night of prayer, without making fun of the prayer. The laugh was at herself. Second, her generosity, and this one is in Bukhari. When she grew older, Sawdah gave her turn, her day with the Prophet, to Aisha. Something she could have held on to, she handed to someone else, freely. Third, how the other wives saw her. In Sahih Muslim, Aisha says she never saw a woman she would rather be in the skin of than Sawdah. Aisha adds, honestly, that Sawdah had a certain sharpness. A real person, then: quick, funny, a little fierce, and generous. And fourth, one more practical scene from Bukhari. At the pilgrimage, Bukhari describes her as heavy and slow-moving, and she asked permission to leave Muzdalifah early, before the crowds. He gave it. Aisha later wished she had asked too. Put these together and Sawdah is remembered less for one great act than for the weather she made in a house: a laugh after a long night, a day handed over, an early start before the crowds. She was the one who made him smile.

Then look for something light you could give them later today. Sawdah's joke was at her own expense. Find one like that: a story on yourself, a silly moment from your week. Hold it ready. If you pray, you can ask that your words lighten someone and wound no one. The bell holds the time.

809.title: Aisha the scholar
809.hook: the companions brought her their hard questions, and she corrected them from the Qur'an and from what she had seen
809.howItsDone: Muslims learning hadith meet Aisha as a narrator again and again, and her corrections of other companions are studied as part of how the early community checked what it heard.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sawdah and her joke about the long bow. Your line was: the one who made him smile. Who got your story on yourself? Day eight hundred nine.

A report is being passed along. It comes from a respected companion, and it says the dead are punished because their families weep for them. Then it reaches Aisha, the Prophet's wife, and she does not simply nod. In the account in Bukhari, she says, in effect: may Allah have mercy on him, but that is not what the Messenger said. And she reaches for the Qur'an to answer it. Today: Aisha the scholar.
screen: `A HARSH REPORT GOES AROUND.` → `IT REACHES AISHA.` → `THAT IS NOT WHAT HE SAID.`

segments.voice: Aisha lived beside the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the small rooms next to the mosque. After his death, people came to her door with questions, and the hadith collections keep her answers. Here is how she answered the report about weeping. She said the Prophet had spoken about a particular person, not about all the grieving. And she pointed to a principle the Qur'an states more than once: no soul carries the burden of another soul. A family's tears cannot be counted against the one they mourn. That is the scholar's move: test what you hear against the text, and against what you witnessed. She did it again when some said a woman passing in front of a man at prayer cuts off his prayer, as a donkey or a dog would. In Bukhari, she answers sharply: you have made us equal to donkeys and dogs. I used to lie stretched out in front of him while he prayed. She was an eyewitness, and she used it. And the companions noticed. Tirmidhi preserves the words of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: whenever a hadith puzzled them, they asked Aisha, and found knowledge with her. Her nephew Urwa learned from her and taught others in turn. A later scholar, al-Zarkashi, gathered her corrections of other companions into a book of their own. So when Muslims speak of the mothers of the believers as teachers, this is a large part of what they mean. A woman at home, with a door that kept opening, and a habit of checking the words. She taught the teachers.

segments.voice: The practice: ask a scholar a question. Settle, and breathe. Think of something about faith, or about this path, that you've heard repeated and never checked. A saying, a rule, a story. Hold it up the way Aisha did. Where does it come from? What does the text actually say? Let the question get sharp and clear. Then think of someone you could ask: a teacher, an imam, a librarian, a good book. If you pray, you can ask for knowledge that helps. The bell holds the time.

810.title: Hafsah, keeper of pages
810.hook: Umar's daughter, in whose house the gathered sheets of the Qur'an were kept (Bukhari)
810.howItsDone: Muslims who study how the Qur'an was gathered learn the reports in Sahih al-Bukhari of Zayd ibn Thabit's collection under Abu Bakr and Uthman's copying from the sheets kept by Hafsah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aisha, who checked what she heard against the text. Your line was: she taught the teachers. Did your question find someone to answer it? Day eight hundred ten.

A messenger knocks at a woman's door with a request from the caliph Uthman. Please send us the sheets, so we can copy them. We will return them to you. What she has in her house is not jewelry and not a treasury. It is a set of written pages, gathered by careful hands, that she has been trusted to keep. The whole community is about to depend on them. Today: Hafsah.
screen: `A KNOCK FROM THE CALIPH.` → `SEND US THE SHEETS.` → `WE WILL RETURN THEM.`

segments.voice: Hafsah was the daughter of Umar ibn al-Khattab and a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Her place in this story comes from two reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, told one after the other. The first is a gathering. After a battle in which many who knew the Qur'an by heart were killed, Umar urged Abu Bakr to collect the Qur'an in writing. Abu Bakr hesitated: how could he do something the Prophet had not done? In the end he agreed, and gave the task to Zayd ibn Thabit. Zayd says it would have been easier to move a mountain. He searched for the verses, gathering them from what was written and from the memories of men. The sheets, Bukhari says, stayed with Abu Bakr until he died, then with Umar for the rest of his life, and then with Hafsah, daughter of Umar. The second report is the knock at her door. In Uthman's time, people in distant lands were reciting differently and arguing over it. Uthman sent to Hafsah, asking for the sheets so they could be copied, with a promise to return them. She sent them. Copies were made and sent out to the regions. And the sheets went back to Hafsah. Look at what kind of honor this is. Hafsah did not write the pages or gather them. She kept them. When the community needed a trusted standard, it knew exactly whose house to ask, and the pages came back to the place they had been safe. Keeping is quiet work, and it is real work. She kept the pages.
screen: `ZAYD GATHERS THE VERSES.` · `ABU BAKR, THEN UMAR, THEN HAFSAH.` · `UTHMAN SENDS TO HER DOOR.` · `THE SHEETS COME BACK TO HER.` · then, large: `SHE KEPT THE PAGES.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep something precious safe. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been trusted with. A letter, a photograph, a recipe, a secret someone told you, a copy of a holy book on your shelf. Picture where it is right now. Is it safe there? Would it come back to you if you lent it? Breathe in, and hold it in mind with care. If you pray, you can give thanks for what has been placed in your keeping. The bell holds the time.

811.title: Umm Salamah
811.hook: her counsel breaks a silence at Hudaybiyyah, and her question is answered by a verse of the Qur'an
811.howItsDone: Muslims recite surah 33:35 as a verse naming believing men and women side by side, and retell Umm Salamah's advice at Hudaybiyyah from Sahih al-Bukhari as an example of wise counsel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hafsah and the sheets that came back to her house. Your line was: she kept the pages. What did you put somewhere safe? Day eight hundred eleven.

Nobody moves. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, has just agreed a treaty at Hudaybiyyah, outside Mecca, and the terms feel to his companions like a defeat. He tells them: get up, sacrifice your animals, and shave your heads. Bukhari says not one of them rose. He says it again. And again. Silence. So he goes into his tent, to his wife, and tells her what has happened. Today: Umm Salamah.
screen: `A TREATY THAT FEELS LIKE DEFEAT.` → `NOT ONE OF THEM ROSE.` → `HE GOES IN TO HIS WIFE.`

segments.voice: Her advice, in Bukhari, is short and wise. Go out, she says, and don't say a word to anyone. Sacrifice your own animal, and call your barber to shave your head. He does exactly that. And when the companions see it, they get up, sacrifice, and start shaving one another, crowding so hard in their distress that it looked as if they might hurt each other. Umm Salamah understood something about grief and pride: people who won't be argued into moving can sometimes be shown. That's the first thing she's remembered for: counsel in a hard hour. The second is a question. In a report in the Musnad of Ahmad, Umm Salamah asks the Prophet: why are we, the women, not mentioned in the Qur'an the way the men are? She doesn't say it in a corner. She asks him directly. And then, the report says, she heard him reciting from the pulpit a new verse, surah thirty-three, verse thirty-five. In Pickthall it begins: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender". And it goes on like that, pair after pair: men who believe and women who believe, men who are truthful and women who are truthful, men who give charity and women who give charity, men who fast and women who fast, all the way to forgiveness and a vast reward. The verse speaks to women and men alike. The report adds a story behind it: someone asked. Her question didn't ask for less from women. It asked to be named. She asked, and it came.

segments.voice: The practice: ask the question that's missing. Settle, and breathe. Think of a room you're part of: a family, a team, a congregation, a class. Is there someone, or something, nobody ever mentions there? Let the question form, as plainly as Umm Salamah's: why isn't this spoken of? You don't have to ask it yet. Just find the words, and hold them. If you pray, you can bring that question to Allah, as she brought hers to the Prophet. The bell holds the time.

812.title: Zaynab bint Jahsh
812.hook: the wives measure their hands to solve a riddle, and the answer turns out to be charity (Muslim)
812.howItsDone: Muslims retell the hadith of 'the longest hand' from Sahih Muslim when speaking of charity, and honor Zaynab bint Jahsh among the mothers of the believers for giving from the work of her hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umm Salamah, who advised silence and asked to be named. Your line was: she asked, and it came. Did you ask your missing question? Day eight hundred twelve.

Who will be first? In Sahih Muslim, Aisha tells it. The Prophet had said to his wives that the one of them with the longest hand would be the quickest to join him after his death. So they measured their hands, side by side, to see whose was longest. It sounds like a party game: wives holding out their arms, comparing fingertips. And they missed what he meant. Today: Zaynab bint Jahsh.
screen: `WHO WILL FOLLOW HIM FIRST?` → `THE LONGEST HAND.` → `THEY MEASURED.`

segments.voice: The wives took the words of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, literally, and looked for the longest arm. But Aisha says the longest hand among them was Zaynab bint Jahsh's, because she used to work with her hands and give in charity. Tradition says she was the first of the wives to follow him in death. The riddle was never about length. It was about reach: how far a person's hands went toward others. In Arabic the phrase is atwalukunna yadan, the longest of you in hand. The report itself shows what a long hand meant: a giving one. Notice where her giving came from. Zaynab didn't only hand over what she had. She made things, the report says, and gave from the work of her own hands. Charity that has your fingerprints on it. Notice also who tells us this. Aisha and Zaynab were rivals in the household; the reports don't hide it. Yet it is Aisha who preserves Zaynab's best memory. In another report in Muslim, Aisha describes her as unmatched in her religion, in her fear of Allah, in truthfulness, in keeping ties of family, and in giving charity. And in the account of the slander against Aisha, Bukhari has Zaynab asked what she knew, and answering that she knew nothing but good of her. The two women spoke well of each other when it counted. The longest hands, it turns out, also reached across a rivalry.
screen: `THEY MEASURED THEIR HANDS.` · `SHE WORKED, AND SHE GAVE.` · `A LONG HAND IS A GENEROUS ONE.` · `RIVALS WHO SPOKE WELL OF EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `THE LONGEST HANDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: give with your own hands. Settle, and rest your hands open on your knees. Look at them. Breathe. Think of one thing those hands could make or do for someone else today. Bake something, mend something, write a note by hand, carry someone's bags, cook a meal to share. Not money from a screen. Something with your fingerprints on it. Choose one, and picture your hands doing it. If you pray, you can ask that your hands reach a little further. The bell holds the time.
Atwalukunna yadan, 'the longest of you in hand,' the riddle about reach, not length, that named Zaynab bint Jahsh, who gave from her own hands' work. Today's word.
Your line: the longest hands. Today, make or do one thing for someone with your own hands, and give it. Day eight hundred twelve.
